articles.title: John Nicks Dies at 97, Figure Skating Hall of Famer Coached Peggy Fleming, Ashley Wagner, More
articles.summary: Legendary figure skating coach John Nicks died Tuesday at the age of 97.
articles.body:
Legendary figure skating coach John Nicks died Tuesday at the age of 97.

"The skating community has lost a tremendous ambassador," U.S. Figure Skating chief executive Matt Farrell said, per the Associated Press' Dave Skretta . "John helped shape generations of American figure skaters and his influence extended well beyond the champions he coached."

Nicks was a decorated skater in his own right. Teaming with sister Jennifer, he won gold in the pairs competition at the 1953 World Championships. They were also silver medalists in 1950 and earned bronze in 1951 and 1952.

Nicks left a larger legacy after pivoting to coaching.

Peggy Fleming, Sasha Cohen, Ashley Wagner and Kristi Yamaguchi are among the decorated skaters he worked with through the years. Skretta noted the overall total eclipsed 1,200 figure skaters.

"Mr Nicks, you were a champion maker," Wagner said in an Instagram post . "I will forever be grateful for my time with you, the lessons learned and the athlete that you transformed me into. You made me understand that I had to skate for the person sitting in the last row, at the top of the arena. You made me a performer, a skater who learned to care so much more about the total package, instead of just the jumps. Thank you for making me a champion, I would not be where I am today if it were not for you."

U.S. Figure Skating inducted Nicks into its Hall of Fame in 1993, and he earned a spot in the World Figure Skating Hall of Fame in 2000.

articles.title: History! 15-year-old Tanvi Patri becomes first Indian woman to reach Youth Olympic badminton final
articles.summary: India's Tanvi Patri scripted history on Wednesday by becoming the first Indian woman to reach the badminton final at the Youth Olympic Games.
articles.body: India's Tanvi Patri scripted history on Wednesday by becoming the first Indian woman to reach the badminton final at the Youth Olympic Games. The 15-year-old defeated Japan's Yuzuno Watanabe 21-14, 11-21, 21-19 in a thrilling three-game semifinal in Buenos Aires. The Odisha shuttler showed great fighting spirit to overcome her opponent and move within one win of a historic gold medal.Tanvi had to work hard for the victory after Watanabe bounced back strongly in the second game. However, the Indian kept her calm in the deciding game and came up with some attacking shots to seal the contest. The victory was also a sweet revenge for Tanvi, who had lost to Watanabe 21-14, 21-10 in their previous meeting in Thailand.Before her, only three Indian shuttlers - HS Prannoy, Lakshya Sen and Aditya Joshi - had reached the badminton semifinals at the competition.Prannoy won silver at the inaugural Youth Olympic Games in Singapore in 2010. Lakshya also finished with a silver medal at the 2018 edition in Buenos Aires. Aditya, meanwhile, reached the boys' singles semifinals in 2014 but returned without a medal.Tanvi has already made a name for herself in junior badminton. She earlier won the girls' singles U-17 title at the Badminton Asia U-17 and U-15 Championships in Chengdu, becoming the first Indian shuttler to win both continental titles.Now, the 15-year-old has a chance to create another piece of history. articles.title: Olympic gold, Asiad medals stolen from hockey legend MM Somaya's Bengaluru home
articles.summary: BENGALURU: Last Wednesday, when hockey legend MM Somaya returned from his morning walk in Apangela, near his hometown Madikeri, his wife Shami greeted him
articles.body: BENGALURU: Last Wednesday, when hockey legend MM Somaya returned from his morning walk in Apangela, near his hometown Madikeri, his wife Shami greeted him with news of a burglary at their Bengaluru residence.His first thoughts were about his most prized possessions - medals won for the country, including his gold medal from 1980 Moscow Olympics. He rushed back to find his worst fears confirmed. His house in HAL 3rd Stage had been broken into between 2.30am and 4am on Oct 28, and valuables worth over Rs 3 lakh, including four international medals, were stolen."I'm obviously very hurt because the medals are an irreplaceable symbol of years of dedication, sacrifice and service to the country," an anguished Somaya told TOI.The two burglars, wearing helmets, also stole Rs 30,000 in cash and gold and silver articles. They entered after breaking open the main door and were captured on neighbours' CCTV cameras."Apart from the Olympic gold, two Asian Games medals - a silver from the 1982 Games in New Delhi and a bronze from the 1986 Games in Seoul - and a Champions Trophy bronze from 1982 were stolen," Somaya (67) added.Neighbours alerted the couple around 7.30am, and they immediately left for Bengaluru. Police registered an FIR the same day and said they were confident of solving the case, citing strong clues."We have collected much CCTV footage from the area and have some vital clues on the miscreants. They had watched the house for some hours and, after ensuring it was locked, broke in. However, we will crack the case," an investigating officer said.Somaya, a former India captain, moved to the city from Mumbai in 2025 after retiring from Bharat Petroleum.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Bengaluru | Silver Rate in Bengaluru | Bank Holidays in Bengaluru | Public Holidays in Bengaluru | Bengaluru AQI | Weather in Bengaluru | Petrol Price in Bengaluru | Diesel Price in Bengaluru | CNG Price in Bengaluru | LPG Price in BengaluruStay updated with the latest Bengaluru news. articles.title: ‘Everybody can play on turf’: Dutch Olympic champion explains where India are falling behind
articles.summary: Mohali: Former Netherlands hockey star Floris jan Bovelander believes India’s vast talent pool can only translate into sustained global success if the
articles.body: Mohali: Former Netherlands hockey star Floris jan Bovelander believes India’s vast talent pool can only translate into sustained global success if the country improves access to artificial turf pitches and strengthens grassroots development programmes.In Punjab for the Asian Champions Trophy, Bovelander, who has been involved in hockey development projects in India for more than a decade, said the biggest difference between hockey powers such as the Netherlands and India remained infrastructure at the grassroots level.“We have more than a thousand turf pitches in the Netherlands and all kids start on turf pitches,” Bovelander said. “The techniques and tactics of modern hockey are easier to learn when you play on turf from a young age.”While India possesses a far larger playing base, he noted that many pitches remain concentrated in stadiums and elite centres, limiting access for young players.“You have pitches, but sometimes you’re not allowed to play on them because they’re in stadiums. In the Netherlands, everybody can play on the turf pitches. That’s important for development,” said the two-time Olympic gold medallist.Bovelander, who helped establish the Naval Tata Hockey Academy in Jharkhand and remains involved in community-based programmes through the Bovelander Foundation, stressed that infrastructure alone was not enough.“There is often a lot of focus on high performance, but high-performance hockey benefits from strong grassroots programmes,” he added. “You need festivals, school competitions, youth leagues and good coaching. Elite players inspire young children, but you also need a strong base underneath.”As for the Indian men’s team, Bovelander said it had developed into one of the world’s most difficult sides to beat, citing back-to-back Olympic bronze medals as evidence of its progress. However, he admitted India had occasionally fallen short in key moments at major tournaments.“They are one of the top teams in the world. Maybe they are missing a little bit in the key moments, but they are always there,” he said. “If things go their way at one of the next major tournaments, they can win.”Bovelander also called for a healthy balance between experienced players and emerging talent, saying national teams should avoid relying on reputation alone.“Players should be in the team because of their performances, not because of their history,” he said. “Young players must keep pushing the experienced ones.”India’s 2016 Junior World Cup-winning generation had gone on to form the backbone of the senior side, he noted, but the challenge now was ensuring the next crop of youngsters was given similar opportunities.As far as his discussions with Punjab’s administration is concerned, Bovelander said he hoped to explore ways of contributing to coaching and grassroots initiatives, adding that expanding access to playing facilities would be among the issues he would raise with policymakers.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates.
